source_text: Πῶς δὲ καὶ κατὰ τίνας ἐπικρατείας διειλημμένα τὰ μέρη τῆς γῆς διοικεῖται ὑπὸ τῶν ἐποπτευόντων αὐτὰ, ὁ βουλόμενος διηγησάσθω· ἀπαγγειλάτω δὲ ἡμῖν καὶ πῶς ὀρθῶς πράττεται τὰ παρ᾿ ἑκάστοις δρώμενα, ὅπῃ τοῖς ἐπόπταις ἐστὶ φίλον, καὶ εἰ ὀρθῶς ἔχουσι φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν οἱ Σκυθῶν περὶ ἀναιρέσεως πατέρων νόμοι ἢ οἱ Περσῶν, μὴ κωλύοντες γαμεῖσθαι τοῖς (οἰκείοις) παισὶ τὰς μητέρας μηδὲ ὑπὸ τῶν πατέρων τὰς ἑαυτῶν θυγατέρας. καὶ τί με δεῖ ἐπιλεγόμενον ἀπὸ τῶν πραγματευσαμένων περὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς διαφόροις ἔθνεσι νόμων προσαπορεῖν, πῶς παρ᾿ ἑκάστοις ὀρθῶς πράττονται, καθὼς τοῖς ἐπόπταις φίλον, οἱ νόμοι; λεγέτω δ᾿ ἡμῖν ὁ Κέλσος, πῶς οὐχ ὅσιον παραλύειν νόμους πατρίους περὶ τοῦ γαμεῖν μητέρας καὶ θυγατέρας. ἢ περὶ τοῦ μακάριον εἶναι ἀγχόνῃ τὸν βίον ἐξελθεῖν, ἢ πάντως καθαίρεσθαι τοὺς ἑαυτοὺς παραδιδόντας τῷ πυρὶ καὶ τῇ διὰ πυρὸς ἀπαλλαγῇ τῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ βίου· καὶ πῶς οὐχ ὅσιον παραλύειν νόμους τοὺς φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν παρὰ Ταύροις περὶ τοῦ ἱερεῖα τοὺς ξένους προσάγεσθαι τῇ Ἀρτέμιδι, ἢ παρὰ Λιβύων τισὶ περὶ τοῦ καταθύειν τὰ τέκνα τῷ Κρόνῳ. πλὴν ἀκολουθεῖ τῷ Κέλσῳ τὸ μὴ ὅσιον εἶναι Ἰουδαίοις παραλύειν νόμους πατρίους τοὺς περὶ τοῦ μὴ δεῖν ἄλλον τινὰ σέβειν θεὸν παρὰ τὸν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργόν. καὶ ἔσται κατ᾿ αὐτὸν οὐ φύσει τὸ ὅσιον ἀλλά τινι θέσει καὶ νομίσει θεῖον· ὅσιον γὰρ παρὰ τοῖσδε μὲν σέβειν κροκόδειλον καὶ ἐσθίειν τῶν παρ᾿ ἄλλοις τι προσκυνουμένων, καὶ ὅσιον ἑτέροις τὸ σέβειν τὸν μόσχον, καὶ παρ᾿ ἄλλοις τὸν τράγον νομίζειν θεόν. οὕτως δ᾿ ἔσται (ὁ) αὐτὸς ὅσια μὲν ποιῶν ὡς πρὸς τούσδε τοὺς νόμους, ἀνόσια δὲ ὡς πρὸς ἑτέρους· ὅπερ ἐστὶ πάντων ἀτοπώτατον.
thought_title: If every ancestral law were holy
pass_a_gloss: How and according to what dominions the parts of the earth, divided, are administered by those overseeing (ἐποπτευόντων) them, let whoever wishes relate (διηγησάσθω); and let him report (ἀπαγγειλάτω) to us also how the things done among each are rightly done, as is dear to the overseers, and whether rightly stand, say (φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν), the laws of the Scythians about the killing (ἀναίρεσις) of fathers or those of the Persians, not forbidding (μὴ κωλύοντες) mothers to be married to their own children (παισί) nor daughters by their fathers. And why need I, gathering (ἐπιλεγόμενον) from those who have treated (πραγματευσαμένων) the laws in the various (διαφόροις) nations, raise further difficulty (προσαπορεῖν), how among each the laws are rightly done, as is dear to the overseers? Let Celsus tell us how it is not holy to abolish ancestral (πατρίους) laws about marrying mothers and daughters, or about its being blessed (μακάριον) to go out of life by hanging (ἀγχόνη), or about those who hand themselves over (παραδιδόντας) to fire and to release (ἀπαλλαγή) from life through fire being wholly purified (καθαίρεσθαι); and how it is not holy to abolish laws, say, among the Taurians about bringing strangers (ξένους) as sacrifices (ἱερεῖα) to Artemis, or among some of the Libyans about sacrificing (καταθύειν) children (τέκνα) to Kronos. However, it follows (ἀκολουθεῖ) for Celsus that it is not holy for Jews to abolish ancestral laws about not needing to revere (σέβειν) any other god besides the craftsman/Maker (δημιουργός) of the universe (τῶν ὅλων). And according to him the holy (τὸ ὅσιον) will be not by nature (φύσει) but by some enactment (θέσει) and custom (νομίσει) divine (θεῖον); for it is holy among these to revere the crocodile and to eat something of what is worshipped (προσκυνουμένων) among others, and holy for others to revere the calf (μόσχος), and among others to think the goat (τράγος) a god. Thus the same man will be doing holy things in relation to these laws, unholy (ἀνόσια) in relation to others; which is the most absurd (ἀτοπώτατον) of all.

pass_b_english: How, and under what dominions, the parts of the earth are divided and administered by those who oversee them, let anyone who wishes explain. And let him tell us also how what is done among each people is done rightly when done in the way that pleases the overseers, and whether, for example, the laws of the Scythians about killing their fathers are right, or those of the Persians, which do not forbid mothers to be married by their own sons, or daughters by their own fathers.

And why need I gather instances from those who have written treatises on the laws of the various nations, and press the difficulty further: how are the laws among each people rightly kept, in the way that pleases the overseers? Let Celsus tell us how it is not holy to abolish ancestral laws about marrying mothers and daughters, or about its being blessed to depart this life by hanging, or about the claim that those who give themselves up to the fire and to release from life through fire are wholly purified. And how is it not holy to abolish laws such as those among the Taurians about offering strangers as sacrifices to Artemis, or among some of the Libyans about sacrificing children to Cronus?

Yet it does follow from Celsus’s view that it is not holy for the Jews to abolish their ancestral laws, which say that one must worship no other god besides the Maker of the universe. And on his account what is holy will be divine not by nature but by some enactment and custom. For among some it is holy to revere the crocodile and to eat something that others worship; among others it is holy to revere the calf; and among others again, to consider the goat a god. And so the same man will be doing holy things with regard to these laws, and unholy things with regard to others; which is the most absurd thing of all.
notes: Echoes of Celsus's phrases ('under certain dominions', 'in the way that pleases', 'it is not holy to abolish') are given in Origen's syntax and not set as fresh quotations, since Origen is now turning them into questions. Scythian parricide and Persian next-of-kin marriage are common ethnographic topics; Origen names no source and none is cited. The Taurian sacrifice of strangers to Artemis is the story of Euripides' Iphigenia among the Taurians and Herodotus 4.103, but Origen cites neither, so no inline source is given. The hanging and fire customs are left unidentified (fire may refer to Indian ascetics). περὶ τοῦ ... πάντως καθαίρεσθαι (article with infinitive) rendered 'about the claim that ... are wholly purified', parallel to 'about its being blessed'. οἰκείοις is Koetschau's supplement, translated as 'their own'. οὐ φύσει τὸ ὅσιον ἀλλά τινι θέσει καὶ νομίσει θεῖον is awkward in Greek (θεῖον may be corrupt or predicative); rendered 'what is holy will be divine not by nature but by some enactment and custom'. σέβειν rendered 'revere' and προσκυνουμένων 'worship', to keep the two verbs apart; τι (the thing eaten) left as 'something', not narrowed to 'creatures'. θεός lower-case in 'no other god' and 'consider the goat a god' (generic and pagan); δημιουργός rendered 'Maker'. (ὁ) is Koetschau's supplement. The Egyptian crocodile and calf cults and the goat of Mendes stand behind the examples. Kronos rendered 'Cronus'. No Scripture quoted.
Open doubt (review): 5.27: οὐ φύσει τὸ ὅσιον ἀλλά τινι θέσει καὶ νομίσει θεῖον is awkward in the Greek, and θεῖον may be corrupt. The rendering stays close to the Greek, and the note flags it.
